frase_gancho.texto: Few pieces of Mixtec gold escaped the conquerors’ fires.

puente_narrativo.texto: From gold we move on to bones. Look for a clay object that looks like a skeleton. It is a human spine standing upright, with its vertebrae stacked one on top of another and traces of orange and red paint.

guion_corto.texto: This stop is devoted to Mixtec goldwork. Many historians consider the Mixtec the finest goldsmiths of Mesoamerica. They melted gold, silver, and copper, mixed them in different proportions to obtain different colors, and cast the metal using the lost-wax technique. In this way they made pectorals, necklaces, rings, bells, and ornaments for the ears and the lip, called lip plugs. Some jewels carry extremely fine threads of metal that outline eyes, claws, or spirals. They were not mere decoration: they showed the rank of the person who wore them. The great treasure of this art came out of Tomb 7 at Monte Albán, which Alfonso Caso discovered in 1932. Today it is displayed mostly in Oaxaca.

guion_largo.texto:
Almost all of the Mixtec’s gold ended up in the fire. The conquerors coveted gold and often melted it down. A jewel that had taken months of work could become a shapeless bar of metal. It was not for lack of admiration: Fray Bernardino de Sahagún, a sixteenth-century friar, described in detail how Indigenous metalworkers did their work. That is why what survived matters so much, and what survived was almost always what lay underground.

In 1932, Alfonso Caso reached Tomb 7 at Monte Albán after breaking through the wall of an elite residence. Inside were more than five hundred objects, and more than one hundred twenty of them were gold. Necklaces, pectorals, rings, ear ornaments, and pendants appeared, mixed with turquoise, rock crystal, carved bone, and other luxury materials. It was one of the richest finds in Mexican archaeology.

Mixtec goldsmiths knew how to blend. They melted gold, silver, and copper in different proportions. According to the INAH restorers who studied the treasure of Tomb 7, this is how they achieved three tones. There was a pale yellow, almost greenish, a golden yellow, and a reddish yellow. Each alloy was chosen according to what the jewel needed, both in strength and in meaning.

You already know the lost-wax technique, the method behind the great pectoral. But there were more resources. Extremely fine threads of metal were used for the details: eyes, fangs, wings, claws, and spirals. Some threads imitated feathers. And bells hung from many jewels. In Tomb 7, sixteen types of bell were identified. More than three thousand six hundred beads were also counted, forming sixty-nine necklaces, bracelets, and strands.

These jewels told who you were. A noble person justified their rank by lineage and by valor in war, and showed it through clothing and ornaments. A pectoral, a lip plug, or a pair of ear ornaments were like an identity card worn on the body. The lip plug, by the way, is an ornament placed in the lip.

Gold rarely came alone. The Mixtec were also masters of mosaic, and they combined gold and turquoise, as in the skull you saw from the same tomb. It is said that turquoise masks were given as gifts to seal alliances. In Zaachila, another city with Mixtec tombs, the principal lord of Tomb 2 wore a gold pectoral. Other figures had bracelets and rings. You already know that city from the [hummingbird cup](mna_s07_vasija_colibri_zaachila).

And not everything stayed in Oaxaca. A gold pendant showing a noble with a lip plug, a staff, and a shield is kept in the British Museum. It was found in the 1870s, in Tehuantepec. There are also Mixtec gold rings in Turin and in Munich. It is another version of the story of Mexican pieces that live far from home, like the Penacho of Vienna.

If you want to see the Tomb 7 ensemble, you will have to travel. Most of it is displayed in the Museum of the Cultures of Oaxaca, in the former convent of Santo Domingo. When you look at the jewels at this stop, think of the ones that are missing, the ones that were melted down. The ones that survive reached you because someone placed them underground, so that no one would touch them.

texto: Look for the bells or pendants hanging from any of the jewels
Notice the extremely fine threads of metal that outline eyes, feathers, or spirals
Compare the color of the jewels: some paler and others more reddish

texto.Material: Gold, silver, and copper in different alloys, often combined with turquoise
texto.Technique: Lost wax and fine metal threads
texto.Origin: Oaxaca (the large Tomb 7 ensemble from Monte Albán is kept in the Museum of the Cultures of Oaxaca)

texto.pregunta: Myth: All the gold from Tomb 7 at Monte Albán is displayed in this museum.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Most of the treasure is in the Museum of the Cultures of Oaxaca, in the former convent of Santo Domingo.
